utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ierace [Continued]:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, yesterday reference was made to the shelling of the city in early June 1992 and the filming of that shelling by your team from the upper floors of the state hospital. How far from the hospital were the Unis towers?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A couple of hundred metres at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask the witness be shown a video clip, which is tab 5.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one stage during that story we saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have to say that the monitors which we have are completely invisible. We cannot go on in this way and something has to be done about it. I'm going to tell the Registry that we cannot have a trial in which the Trial Chamber cannot see what is on the monitor. Now, I don't know what's to be done. I'm going to make some inquiries now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you see anything, Baron, there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very dark, Your Honour, indeed, because certainly the early shots in that story were daylight, and it looks like it's in the middle of the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point is this, that the evidence loses all its impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know why it can't be done. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The only suggestion I could make for today's purposes is to indicate which video clips I would otherwise have shown and for the Bench to view those in Chambers and questions to be asked as to their content after that. Your Honour, perhaps another suggestion: We don't have a problem with our monitor at the bar table. I wonder if there was a short adjournment we might receive some technical assistance and adjust the monitors on the Bench, in particular the contrast, to maximise the picture that they're capable of producing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many clips do you have, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Four altogether, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's the angle of the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, some improvement might be made. Judge Kwon helpfully suggests a change in the monitor. Certainly it's a bit clearer. But of course the result is that one cannot see the rest of the court. An absurd situation. But in any event, we can't waste time. What we can do is to view these clips in due course in Chambers. We will play them now and try and see what we can, and if anything arises from it, as I say, we can view them in due course, which we will do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Baron, in that clip you were seen facing the camera. Were you in the upper stories of the state hospital at that point?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the top floor of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was some footage as well of some patients. Do you know where that footage was taken?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Taken in the Kosevo hospital, the main academic hospital of Sarajevo, the following morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as best as you are able, when was that story filmed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of June 1992, the 5th or 6th or 7th of June. I don't recall the precise date, but it was in the early days of June, after the evacuation by the Yugoslav army from the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that video clip tab 2 now be screened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In yesterday's summary of your evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I must, having complained earlier, there is an improvement, at least as far as my monitor is concerned, but let's go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In yesterday's presentation of your evidence on an earlier occasion, reference was made to an incident when you were driving along the Marsal Tito Boulevard and observed a high-rise apartment block come under fire. Does the footage we've just viewed relate to that incident?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reference was also made to an observation by you that the incendiary rounds continued to hit the building at a lower level than the firemen were as they attempted to put out the fire. Did you draw any conclusions from your observations in that regard?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I felt that what was being done was that the civilian services, the fire services, were themselves being targeted. Having reached the fires in the upper stories of that building, fires were then caused by the incendiary rounds in the lower stories, and my conclusion was that they were trying to trap the firemen at the top of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that footage filmed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 5th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness now be shown tab 5.9, a further video clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As best as you recollect, when was that footage shot?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the Jewish cemetery in relation to the confrontation lines between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a sort of no man's land between the warring parties, right on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the last minute or so of that story we appeared to see the view available through a space in a Serb position, a Bosnian Serb position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The camera appeared to show successive telephoto shots of what could be seen through that space; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the area of the city that one could see through that space?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marin Dvor square, the heart of the city where the Holiday Inn hotel is, the parliament, that area of the town. And the Unis towers were also clearly visible. That had been shown in the first story that you showed, then burning, by that stage of course destroyed, because this was later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at any stage in 1992, did you interview General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts did that interview take place?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interview itself took place at an artillery position to the east of Sarajevo overlooking the city. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the interview recorded on film or video?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that we now see video clip tab 5.8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the video of the interview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your narration, you referred to the General saying that he held the city in his palm.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say that to you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said that as we were walking there but when the cameraman was not actually filming him and me, and it was translated to me by the local producer I had with me. Apart from that, he actually tapped the palm of his hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were living in the upper floors of the state hospital and made observations of shelling of the city, had you ever seen any rounds appear to emanate from that part of the city surrounds?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Bosnian side towards the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any, no. We were there up all night, night after night, and we did not see anything emanating from the places -- any fire emanating from the places around us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen any fire appearing to come from that area, that is the area where you conducted this interview?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we actually filmed it on one occasion in the late afternoon, early evening, again at the beginning of June 1992. Rocket fire, multiple rocket launcher fire. And as far as I'm aware, I was taken to that precise position when I did the interview with General Mladic. This is to the east of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall what the rockets hit, if anything, in the city?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They appeared not to be aimed at one particular target, and we have footage of those rockets hitting the city, and these -- initially in the eastern half of the city. Only later did the fire become more concentrated on the Marsal Tito barracks, which had been evacuated. But while there was concentrated fire on the Marsal Tito barracks, there was also fire all across the city which was not just at one particular point but spread all over the city. So not at one particular target but simply targeting the city as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you interview Dr. Karadzic from time to time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met Dr. Karadzic on several occasions. At the London conference in August 1992, in Belgrade at the beginning of September 1992, and then in Pale repeatedly in September 1992, including several long meetings of three or four hours in the evenings. And the last time that I met him was in February 1994 when I made my last visit to Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had Dr. Karadzic ever expressed to you off camera his views as to the nature of the Bosnian Serbs' claim on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the various conversations I had with him in Pale in September 1992, he repeatedly said that basically the whole city belonged to the Serbs, that it was all Serb territory. He had many maps on his desks, and he appeared to have coloured them in as to what was Serb land and what was non-Serb land, but Sarajevo he considered to be completely Serb, and he said that repeatedly. He also made one remark, saying, "Well, maybe we will have to compromise, but we cannot live with those people." And then he made a comment that surprised me and shocked me, because he said, "A wall should be built through Sarajevo." And you must remember that this was less than three years after the fall of the Berlin wall, a moment in which I think generally around the world everybody rejoiced that a city that had been divided in such a cruel manner had finally become one again, and now Dr. Karadzic was suggesting that a new wall should be built. I was pretty outraged by the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever explain to you his attitude towards Bosnians of the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did in a rather crude manner. He basically said that they were not Slavs and that they were Turks and made various crude remarks as to why he believed that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever interview Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. At the end of July 1991, during the war in Croatia, I was granted an interview with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever express to you, off camera, any views that he held as to the political situation in the region at the time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We held the interview which, as I recall, lasted something like 40 minutes. Certainly more than 30 because the cameraman had to change tapes and the tapes in the betacam camera lasted 30 minutes, so it lasted around 40 minutes. Mr. Milosevic then invited me into another room to share a glass of whisky with him, and there there were no more cameras so this was not part of the official interview and we had a more relaxed discussion. And then he said, "You must understand that we Serbs are being threatened" by what he called a papist German Fourth Reich, an Islamic fundamentalist conspiracy against the Serb people, which he said was led by Hans Dietrich Genscher, the then German foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you form any view, when you heard those comments, as to what his ultimate intentions might be?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apart from finding it slightly ludicrous that the Vatican is put together with Islamic fundamentalists, it was an indication both to me and to the producers who were with me - and these are local producers - that the intention was, it seemed to us, to take the war from Croatia into Bosnia and into Kosovo once the war in Croatia had been finished in a manner that the Serbs wanted it done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Kosovo, either on or off camera, did you question him as to his attitude towards Kosovars?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the interview - this is the actual interview on camera - Mr. Milosevic did his best, and did a pretty good job at it, of basically evading my questions. But when I put it to him that while he demanded certain rights for the Serb minority in Croatia, he had behaved in precisely the opposite manner when it came to the Albanian population in Kosovo. They -- this had been an autonomous province with its own member of the Federal Presidency of Yugoslavia, and the rights of the Albanian majority in Kosovo had, under President Milosevic's rule of Serbia, been taken away, and I said that these two -- that, you know it didn't fit, you couldn't ask for one thing and take it away from somebody else elsewhere. It was the only moment during the interview that Mr. Milosevic became a little angry, and he made it very clear that Kosovo was Serb in his opinion, that it would remain Serb, and that the two issues in his opinion were not linked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in 1994, following the Markale market incident in early February, did you spend any time in Sarajevo or on the Bosnian Serb side in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the massacre occurred, I was in Central Bosnia. To drive from Central Bosnia into Sarajevo, you have to cross Serb lines, and it was made clear to our bureau chief in Belgrade who came down to Pale that the Bosnian Serb leadership would not allow me to cross immediately into Sarajevo. It wanted me to come to Pale first. So that's what we did. We sent a -- Sky News sent another team into Sarajevo itself and I went to Pale and spent the first couple of weeks after the massacre in Pale during which NATO, of course, gave its first ultimatum to the Serbs which led to the 20-kilometre exclusion zone for heavy weaponry around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware of any indications of Serb solidarity in the face of the aftermath of the Markale massacre as you call it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were told that Vojislav Seselj, the extreme nationalist leader in Belgrade had come down to Pale, but I did not personally see him, but we were told by people within the Bosnian Serb Presidency, and I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. personally witnessed that Milan Martic, who was then the leader of the Serbs in Croatia came to Pale and together with Radovan Karadzic inspected a guard of honour in the snow outside what was the Bosnian Serb Presidency in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever given any information as to whether there were any meetings that took place from time to time between Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic, and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was clear that they were meeting during the London conference. And when I met Dr. Karadzic in the Intercontinental Hotel in Belgrade in September 1992 prior to going down to Pale, he told me that he was there also to meet Mr. Milosevic. From other sources both in Pale and in Belgrade, I was told that there were regular meetings between the two men, sometimes with General Mladic present, sometimes not. I was also told that there were meetings just between General Mladic and Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred earlier to conversations that you had with Dr. Karadzic and interviews indeed that you conducted with him. Was he ever forthcoming about the content of the meetings that he had with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. We did ask him on various occasions what he thought Mr. Milosevic thought of any particular development, and he told us that he couldn't talk about such matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you understand that at some stage during the conflict an embargo was placed by Serbian authorities on the movement of goods from Serbia into Bosnian Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As best as you recollect, when was that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: April, May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any observations as to whether the embargo was carried out, and if so, what were those observations?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the period after the Bosnian Serb parliament had rejected the Vance-Owen Peace Plan for Bosnia, and the Bosnian Serbs then organised a referendum on the decision of the Bosnian Serb parliament. My understanding was that Mr. Milosevic had ordered an embargo to prove his anger with the Bosnian Serb parliament for not following his advice and accepting the Vance-Owen peace plan and that he had ordered an embargo of oil and fuel in particular. An embargo within an embargo, because Serbia at that stage was under an UN embargo. But when we drove into northern parts of Eastern Bosnia, we went to a village called Janja and we went into the town of Bijeljina, we saw at various points trucks of various sizes still entering Serb-held parts of Bosnia from Serbia proper. We also saw oil tankers going in, petrol tankers going in. So therefore, leaving us the conclusion that the embargo was one in name only and wasn't being really upheld, and it was an open joke later on in Belgrade that of course this was not really happening but that this was a political move to try and prove something to the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Reference was made yesterday in terms of your earlier evidence to you covering the conflict in Croatia in 1991. Did you notice any similarity between uniforms that you saw in 1991 outside Sarajevo and those that you saw being worn by Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Sarajevo in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. When you were in Sarajevo or at least on Bosnian Serb-held territory in 1992 and made observations as to the uniforms, how did those uniforms compare to those worn by soldiers that you'd seen in 1991?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the same. The only thing was that there was now a cap badge which had the colours of Serbia, white, blue and red. But the uniforms were absolutely identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst there, did you meet any JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met a number officers, including -- I think he was then a major, I think he's now a colonel, Sljivancanin. I've probably mispronounced the name. My excuses for that. And the last few days of the siege we spent all our time with a unit of the 1st Armoured Brigade of the Guards, and there there were a number of officers, including one called Mladen Maric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you receive any information as to whether any of those officers later surfaced in the context of the conflict in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We spent quite some time with Mladen Maric and indeed even went out to dinner in Belgrade with him and some of his men after the fall of Vukovar, and in June 1992, my producer who had been with me in Vukovar told me that he had seen Mladen Maric at the Lukavica barracks on the edge of Sarajevo in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your information, if any, as to the capacity in which he was present in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there as an officer of the Yugoslav army. My understanding was, from what I was told by my producer, that he and his unit, which were just about the best units within the Yugoslav army, were there to try or to prepare for a strike into Sarajevo, which we understood was a strike towards the Marsal Tito barracks and to cut the city in two. That did not go ahead because then an accord was reached and the Marsal Tito barracks were evacuated. My understanding of what happened to -- or he was then a captain, a first captain in the Yugoslav army -- was that although he originally came from Bosnia, he refused to become an actual member of the Bosnian Serb army and returned to Serbia proper, and as far as I'm aware, he is still in what is now the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And was Marsal Tito barracks positioned at the narrowest point of the valley floor?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in autumn 1991, did you report on the conflict in the area south of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that in the vicinity of Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cavtat Yes, indeed. We flew into Montenegro. We had permission from the Yugoslav army to accompany them up -- from Montenegro up the coastal road that leads to Dubrovnik. We passed through several villages that had been razed to the ground, and the forests in this area had also been burnt and it was a sign to us that there was simply a scorched-earth policy on the part of the Yugoslav army. We passed the airport and then came to the outskirts of Cavtat, which is a small town or large village with a natural harbour, and a very beautiful place it is, and there there was still some shooting going on, although I only saw fire from the Yugoslav army, including, somewhat to my amazement, from a T-33 tank. This is tank of -- Soviet tank from the Second World War. We then followed the troops as they entered Cavtat. As I say, I didn't see any sign of resistance but there may have been some before we arrived. In the town we then spoke to some civilians, and we witnessed that at least ten inhabitants of Cavtat were taken away by the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've said that you saw no signs of resistance from the town. Did you see any steps taken to impede their advance further north?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in Cavtat, by the harbour there was an extremely loud explosion. We couldn't immediately see what this was because there were houses between us and the site of the explosion. When we got to higher territory, we saw what we imagined had been an explosion caused by the Croat forces to block the main coastal road leading further north from Cavtat to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ten men, or the ten people you describe as civilians, what was it that led you to the conclusion that they were indeed civilians?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spoke to one of them before he was taken away, in his bar. He was -- he ran a bar. They were all in civilian clothes. We were given Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the names of all ten of them, which we wrote down, and after they were taken away, and we got no more further information as to why they were being taken away, I did a small report and handed it in to the International Committee of the Red Cross in Belgrade that we had witnessed these ten people - ten, it may be 11, it may be nine - and that's the last I heard of it until I returned to Cavtat in 1994 and met the bar owner again. He was still the owner of the bar, but he was a man in pretty bad psychological state. He told me that he had been held for several months and that he had been severely beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever question any leaders of the Serb community as to the reason for the attack on the wider Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in Cavtat, two senior Yugoslav officers arrived there. As I recall, one from the army and from the navy. We did speak to them, but they wouldn't speak to us. They wouldn't answer our question as to why this attack was being done, because this was not an area where Serbs lived, nor is Dubrovnik a town where Serbs lived, apart from one or two. We never got an answer from other officers on that particular trip. We also, of course, asked people in Belgrade as to why Dubrovnik, one of the great cities, a pearl, and I suspect the best known, worldwide, city from the former Yugoslavia was being attacked in this manner which we felt was extremely detrimental to the Serb cause, and I never caught a clear answer from anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the most senior person that you recall posing that question to?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, in -- who was a very close associate of Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his response?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave no response. Again, he wouldn't answer the question. The question was simple: "Why are you allowing the Yugoslav army to attack Dubrovnik? What's the sense of this?" And he simply shook his head and wouldn't answer the question. This was not in a formal interview, I should add, Your Honours. We ran into Mr. Jovic during a conference and managed to speak to him for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same year as your observations in Dubrovnik, in the Dubrovnik area in 1991, did you cover the conflict in the Banja area of Croatia? In particular, did you enter the village of Struga?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was anything happening at around that time, either before or after you entered that village that you observed?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, this was in July 1991. It was my first day in covering the war that was going on in Croatia. We entered -- crossed from Bosnia into Croatia very early in the morning, and we'd been told that there had been fighting in this village called Struga, which lies close to a larger village or small town called Dvor na Uni. We drove into Struga. There we discovered a unit from the Yugoslav army who verified that there had been a shooting going on, who told us, and this is a Serb officer who I later encountered in Bosnia, that Serb militiamen had entered the village of Struga during the night, from Friday to Saturday morning, and indiscriminately opened fire on the houses. As I recall, at least four villagers in Struga were killed. Most of the rest of the population fled. Some of them had shot back because two Serb militiamen had been killed. The JNA officer told me that they had only been sent or only arrived in Struga as a buffer between the two sides after the shooting was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your assessment as to that explanation by him as to his presence?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, one -- I can't give a definitive explanation, but we had a sense that there was some coordination between the Serb militia and the JNA and that the arrival of the JNA so late, only when the fighting had stopped and the militia had withdrawn, that the two were in touch with each other. That was certainly also the opinion of the Croat villagers in Struga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you're able to answer the following questions fairly briefly because we are short of time. In that area did you come across at all Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him in Dvor na Uni on the same day that I had entered Struga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that on one occasion or more than one occasion that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I met him on several occasions after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of those encounters after, as you understood it, he carried out some arrests of some local Serb people?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Several days after this incident in Struga, we had agreed to meet Captain Dragan in Dvor na Uni. When we arrived there, we encountered him and he told us that he had arrested ten local Serbs for what he said was butchering four Croat women in the clinic in Dvor na Uni. Those Croat women had come from the village of Struga. And he said that that kind of behaviour was unacceptable because it was the same kind of behaviour that the Croats had used again the Serbs during the Second World War and therefore that he had arrested them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the response of local Serbs to those arrests as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was extremely tense. Captain Dragan, who had his own militia based in the town of Knin, had put those militiamen around the building in which he was holding these ten Serbs, and -- but there were also villagers there who were clearly angry and who wanted those ten men released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of that incident?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after several hours, a man who I didn't immediately recognise but whom I was later introduced to as Milan Martic arrived, and he ordered, during a rather heated argument between the two men, he ordered Captain Dragan to release the ten Serbs and that's what Captain Dragan did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any observations as to the command and control that Captain Dragan exercised over his forces?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His forces seemed more disciplined and better trained than other militiamen. They wore different uniforms. They were all in one uniform. They had guns from various parts of the world, not just Kalashnikovs. He was clearly in command of his men, but he clearly came under the command of Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask him how he was financed, where he received his weaponry from, his support?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one asks questions like that, but one doesn't always expect an answer, and I didn't get one on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him who ultimately was in charge in terms of his operation?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him who was in charge of what the Serbs were trying to achieve, and his answer was Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes examination-in-chief of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I think we haven't admitted the package including the transcript yet. 540?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would be grateful for a number for all of that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van Lynden, I should first of all like to ask you to take a look at some footage together, some of the ones you brought.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before we do so, Mr. May, I have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. received several of these CDs, and this one here where it says "van Lynden Compilation," is empty. So I wasn't able to establish what was on that CD, but that doesn't matter. I can still ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- go ahead with my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, can you help us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there have been some technical difficulties in producing CDs of the video clips, but I'm surprised to hear that there is still a problem. Perhaps if we could have access to that CD, we could make some further inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let them have it back, Mr. Milosevic, and we'll see what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But regardless of that, there's enough other material to be getting along with, so I can do without the compilation, I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I have here this other CD. It says V0000870, and 000/0871. On your film -- actually that was footage by night, wasn't it, showing the one we saw in 000870/1, that's the one I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the numbers are going to help anybody, but you can describe the clip you want to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that as I've been given very precise data from the CD, I don't know how I could use it otherwise but by giving the numbers of that CD if I want to have it shown, the clip shown. But with respect to this first question, it needn't be shown because we all had a chance of seeing it, and the fact that the town was shelled is not in dispute. We can see the incendiary bullets flying around in different directions and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we've seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tracer bullets.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of which story Mr. Milosevic is referring to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you be specific, Mr. Milosevic. What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to precisely the footage on 0870/1 and the positions ranging from 000 to 00048, that particular section and clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which of the clips that was shown? Is it the first clip that was shown this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm talking about this other CD, the one that was given me. The one we saw this morning, as you were able to see, was quite invisible, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is the following, Mr. van Lynden: Tell me, please, was this an exchange of gunfire between the Muslim forces and the Serb forces? Is that what it was about or was it just one-sided, fire from one side, from the Serb positions, what you observed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness will not be able to say what you're talking about. Let's see if we can get at it another way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in that case, I should like you -- them to have this CD played, because I'm going to ask questions pertaining to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can put it in the machine over there. The CD is 000/0870, and it also says V000871. That's the other marking on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that clip 870 is 12 minutes and 15 seconds long. We can play it, of course, if it's required; and I suspect that the second clip, 871, is of a similar length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us start by playing the first clip and then we will see how we get on. If necessary, we can break into it. Just a moment, Mr. Milosevic. Let us get on with this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first clip is from 000 to 00048.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's up to 48. My question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes. Go on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Was this an exchange of fire or one-way shelling of the town?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, I should explain that this is a half-hour compilation that I did for the end of the year 1992 about the war in Bosnia as a whole. Secondly, the pictures of the shelling you see are all from the early days of June 1992, after the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks, and those pictures show only incoming fire to the Bosnian-held parts of the Bosnian capital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Immediately after that on this same footage, up until 01:02 -- from where we stopped up to 01:02, we see daytime shots of a coffee bar in Sarajevo, men having drinks. Was that the next day after the battles, after these battles? Was that the following day?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were pictures taken not by my own crew but by other crews, as far as I recall, prior to the war in Bosnia beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they follow immediately after this footage of the shelling. So that is why I assumed you filmed it after that. Tell me, what is the date of what you showed on these clips?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered that somebody else -- somebody else filmed those clips.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to move on on this same CD, 01:08. Could you please stop the V000870/1. And we see citizens taking part in a referendum. Could you show us that part of this clip; 01:08 from the footage 0870/1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you stop there, please, and turn it back to the poster for the referendum. Will you wind back the tape to show the ballot paper. The poster that we saw for the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The poster, please. That one. Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say here on this poster? We saw a moment ago it says "referendumi", and on this ballot paper, as far as I can read it, it says "letervoten." What language is this? In what language is this ballot paper?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the interpreters can tell us what language this is in. My impression is that these are shots from a referendum at Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the interpreters to give evidence. It may be that somebody can help as to what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may try and explain. When this end of year documentary was made, I was not actually there when it was edited, when the pictures were put over my words. I was in Bosnia when I wrote this, and the voice tapes, my voice tapes, were sent back to our office in London and the pictures were put over. My understanding was that these were pictures taken again by others, because I was not in Bosnia when the referendum took place. And if these pictures are -- do not match my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. words, then I apologise, but I was not personally responsible because others in London were responsible for that. But that's a possible explanation as to why, if the two don't match.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand your explanation, but the question of authenticity of what is being shown arises, because obviously this is a shot of a referendum in Kosovo. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Albanian language could not have been used on the ballot paper.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I'm not aware. I wasn't there with the editing. And if that was so, then it was a mistake and not anything but a simple mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. van Lynden, that you are aware that prior to that referendum and prior to the proclamation of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that referendum which was held without the participation of the Serbs, there were no conflicts in Bosnia. I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at position 01:20 from this same CD. I want to ask you whether it is quite clear that it shows men on barricades. 01:20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are men on the barricades, are they not? Tell me, were they Serbs who were armed and who erected these barricades or someone else?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that they were Serbs. Again, I was not present in the city. This is an overview, a general overview of what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what part of town -- of the town of Sarajevo were these barricades erected?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't film this, so I wasn't there. So I couldn't tell you with any precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at position 02:20 from the same CD, 02:20.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 02:20, not 01:47. 02:20.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not possible with this software to fast forward with the picture being visible on the screen. One was to get and place the cursor where one anticipates it might be. So we'll do our best.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking you to fast forward, not back. 02:20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to have to deal with this better. Can we simply play this compilation? I wonder if that would be the best and then the accused can ask his questions. Is that going to be a possibility? Because otherwise, we're never really going to get on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It's easily done, Your Honour. It will take 12 minutes and 15 seconds to play it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, play it on to the next part that he wants to ask a question about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop it there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not -- just play it on until we get to the part you want to ask a question about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop here, please. Stop here, please. I wanted the picture to remain on the screen, please, just to see the still, please, so we can see what it is. Could you enlarge it a little? A moment ago one could see quite clearly what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That can't be done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two seconds prior to this, there was a close-up of this same scene.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop there, please. Freeze.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these JNA soldiers? What you describe as the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks, but in fact it was a massacre that occurred during the evacuation, when the column was attacked in Dobrovoljacka Street at the beginning of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're confusing two different evacuations, Mr. Milosevic. There was indeed some kind of an ambush and shooting in May 1992 at the beginning with the evacuation of another barracks. I was not in the city at that stage. I was in the city when the Marsal Tito barracks were evacuated, and I am not aware of any JNA soldiers coming under fire then. Again, these pictures were taken by other cameramen at a stage when I was not in Sarajevo. And once again, just to explain to Your Honours, this is a compilation made over my words by editors who were not under my control because I was working in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regardless of that, as you are providing the commentary for the evacuation of the barracks and the ambush for JNA soldiers, the JNA was leaving the barracks and there was an ambush in Dobrovoljacka Street?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have been told before you must not misrepresent what the witness said. He said that on this occasion when the Marsal Tito barracks were evacuated, there was no ambush and no soldiers were killed. Now, that's what he said. You must pay attention to what he said and ask your questions accordingly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May, but he also said that during the previous evacuation there was an ambush that the soldiers fell into and that a number of them were killed. And this was at the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that right, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. van Lynden, that up until then, there had been no shelling of Sarajevo until that attack on the JNA? That is, up until the beginning of May. Up until that event that took place at the beginning of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was not in the city beforehand, Mr. Milosevic. I only arrived at the end of May 1992. I'm certainly aware of reports that there was fighting in Sarajevo. As to the level of shelling, I can't report about anything that I wasn't there for. I can tell you what happened after I was in Sarajevo. But there was certainly fighting in Sarajevo before that incident of the ambush of the soldiers leaving another barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't ask you whether there was fighting in Sarajevo. I asked you whether there had been any shelling. Namely, I have in mind -- I am not trying to confuse you. I have in mind a statement by General Nambiar, and I'm sure you followed these things as you were a reporter, who said that there had been no shelling before the 3rd of May when this massacre occurred in Dobrovoljacka Street, that the shelling started after that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't argue with the general. If he said that, then -- I mean, I wasn't in the city so I cannot say whether there wasn't or wasn't. All I am aware is that there was fighting going on. So whether that was with heavy shelling or not, but there was fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. van Lynden, what you are showing, that is the actual shelling, it dates to -- the date is June 1992. That means after these events and the conflicts that occurred during the withdrawal from the barracks. I think the date is not in dispute. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, the pictures at the beginning of this story date from the beginning of June 1992. I don't dispute those dates, nor do I dispute this happened at the beginning of May, but again, I was not there for that. But the pictures of the shelling that were shown do come after that event indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this morning, describing the battles around the Jewish cemetery, which you describe as no-man's land, that the fiercest battles were held around the Jewish cemetery, on both sides of the Jewish cemetery. Is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told both from the Bosnian side and from the Bosnian Serb side when I visited those front lines that there had indeed been extremely heavy fighting there. But the company commander who was shown, that I accompanied earlier, in one of the earlier clips shown by Mr. Ierace, had told me that at that stage that section, that front was quieter than it had been before. And that conversation took place with that major in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I was referring to what you -- I noted down when you said that the fiercest fighting was around the Jewish cemetery. As you are testifying as a war reporter, the two sides were in conflict there, were they not?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't a one-sided attack, but there was a conflict between two sides and that was where the front line was. Isn't that right, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting between two sides at the front at the Jewish cemetery, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. On this CD of yours which is now in the machine, at position 02:49, you can see Jusuf Juka Prazina being wounded and leaving a building. I assume it's a hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see it, Your Honour, before I can say whether it is Jusuf Prazina or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, that is Jusuf Prazina. I'm not sure that this shows him leaving a hospital. It shows him walking with crutches on the street. I did once encounter Mr. Prazina during a visit to the Kosevo hospital when he was having his wounds looked at, but he had been wounded at the beginning of the war, prior to my arrival in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that -- do you know that he was an infamous Sarajevo criminal?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the word "infamous," but I know that he was a criminal. He admitted to me, and in the one story that I did about him I said this in the text, that he had had at least five sentences to prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is he also called Juka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is. Yes, that was how he was known; Juka. His official name was Jusuf Prazina, and as far as I'm aware, he was found shot dead in Belgium in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a whole story about him and showed him like some sort of hero, a modern Robin Hood of Sarajevo, distributing toys and humanitarian aid. Isn't that right, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did a story about him. Whether he is a hero in that story or not is up to the viewer. I know from people who do not come from the Balkans, who were surprised at this story that I had done, because I had also said that in the early days of the war he's one of the principal defenders of Sarajevo, and I make quite clear in the story that he was a criminal, and they did not see this as me making him into some kind of a hero. He did go around town and had the odd habit of opening the boot of his car and handing toys to children. We'd simply filmed the reality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, are you aware of another rather unusual habit that he had, and that is to kill Serbs around Sarajevo, apart from distributing toys to children? It is by this other activity that Juka Prazina and his criminals are known by.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him kill any Serbs in Sarajevo. Let me answer the question. You asked me a question. I'll answer it. I never saw him kill any Serbs. In amongst his men were Bosnian Serbs. It wasn't a purely Muslim unit. There were also Croats in that unit. And as far as that is concerned, his unit mirrored Sarajevan society in 1992. I make no claims that he did not murder Serbs. All I'm saying is that I did not witness it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I certainly believe you didn't see him do that, killing anyone, but do you know, since yesterday you mentioned that you didn't get permission to see prisons on the Bosnian side in Sarajevo, do you know how many private and official prisons for Serbs there were in Sarajevo during the time of those battles in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any precise number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have a precise number. I can understand that. But do you have any idea regarding the number of those prisons, any kind of idea, even a most vague one?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't give a figure. But, Mr. Milosevic, if I may just add that while I asked the Bosnian authorities repeatedly throughout the war to be given access to those prisons, I also did the same on the other side of the front line and was only given access once to one prison. When I visited both the Bihac enclave and the Gorazde enclave, respectively in 1994 and 1993, I was given access to two prisons in both those enclaves, but in Sarajevo no. I couldn't give you any figure. I would just be guessing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Serbs did allow you to have access to two prisons with prisoners of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To one prison and not with any prisoners of war. These were people who had been arrested prior to the war in Hadzici in April 1992. None of them ever fought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a regular prison, was it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. It was at Kula. It was not a regular prison. The prisoners were forced to work. These were all civilians that had been rounded up by the Serb authorities in Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on the Muslim side they wouldn't let you see a single prison?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the Bosnian side, both in the Gorazde enclave at the beginning of 1993 and in the Bihac enclave in November-December 1994, I was given access to prisons where I saw prisoners of war from the Bosnian Serb side wearing uniform. I'm not saying that there were not other prisons in Gorazde or Bihac - there may well have been - but I was given access to one in each.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, look at position 04:43:16. 04:43:16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does one see there crosses in several places? In fact, you show funerals and the cries of Serbs and large scale funerals of Serbs. You have this in several places in your features. Isn't that right, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pictures that have just gone by were pictures take in Dobrinja at the beginning of July. This is on the outskirts of Sarajevo, by the airport. Beginning of July 1992, where the siege within the siege was so harsh that the people could only bury their dead at night and not in a proper cemetery but by the roadside. What you saw there was a mixture of Serb, Croat, and Bosnian Muslim dead, therefore buried under different symbols, both crosses and non-crosses. But, yes, I have also witnessed funerals on the Bosnian Serb side. The one that sticks in my mind would be the one in Vlasenica in -- again in September 1992, when, if I'm correct, 28 Bosnian Serb soldiers were killed in the front lines somewhere around the Bosnian enclave of Srebrenica. And that was indeed a mass funeral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the only mass funeral on the Serb side that you filmed. Isn't that right, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, that's the only mass. I mean, I filmed in Dvor na Uni back in July 1991 a funeral of two people. I filmed various funerals in Belgrade in 1991, of soldiers who had been killed in the fighting. But as far as a mass funeral is concerned, that's the only one that I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be a convenient moment. It's time for the break. Let me make two administrative announcements. We will give an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. oral ruling on the preparation of the Defence case at a convenient time during the first session tomorrow, Wednesday, or if there is no convenient time, before the first break. Secondly, we will admit the statement of Witness B-1543 under Rule 92 bis, the witness meeting the various requirements; however, the witness must be present for cross-examination. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered, Mr. Milosevic, how long you should have for cross-examination in all the circumstances of this case. We will give you longer than the Prosecution had. There is a transcript also. The upshot is we will give you another hour and ten minutes, if you require it. If you don't, of course, we'll go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, you explained that a part of the footage shown was not taken by your crew, your team, but you took over other people's footage and clips; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this one story that you have been asking the Court to show, that is correct. In this half hour that I wrote but was not present at the editing of at the end of 1992, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But the comments were yours, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the script, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the script, did you write, for example, where you can see the dead soldiers of the JNA, that they had in fact been killed? Did you say that they were killed withdrawing without putting up any struggle from Sarajevo, without any fighting? They were brutally killed on the occasion. Did your script and comments run in that direction? I didn't notice that you did.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the script in front of me, but I don't recall doing so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't say that. And when showing the graves, you didn't say that they were Serb graves as well, did you? You said a moment ago that there were Serb, Muslim, and Croatian and I don't know what other kind of graves you mentioned, but you didn't say these included Serb graves, did you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in relation to those graves in Dobrinja. They were Bosnian graves, Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Croat, Bosnian Muslim. I didn't have to say they included Bosnian Serb. And I should remember -- remind you that this was on the Bosnian side of the front lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but Serbs were killed there too, and you didn't deny that, did you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't deny that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, you're not commenting and saying that it was the soldiers who were killed without any fighting and were pulled out, and the Serb graves either. Now, in your comments, in your commentary, do you distort the actual image of what was going on in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did. Again, I have to point out to you that I was not there when the pictures were put over my words. Therefore, I was not even aware that the pictures that you showed earlier of JNA soldiers lying dead in the streets were going to be put in over my words. I was working in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I assume that since you were a journalist and since you lived for a time in Belgrade as well or, rather, stayed in Belgrade for some time, that you knew full well that when it was a question of the shelling of Sarajevo that Serbia from top level on several occasions condemned the shelling of Sarajevo, but you say nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of those comments having been made, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. van Lynden. Now, in paragraph 1 of your statement, you say that you knew that in the course of 1991 and 1992, Sky News broadcast on channel 3 of -- was broadcast over channel 3 of Radio-Television Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness, before answering, have a copy of the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Not 24 hours a day, but I believe up to 12 hours per day. I believe also this third channel was only available within Belgrade or the larger Belgrade area. I don't think it was available in the whole of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. How far it could be seen can be established, but it was state Radio-Television Serbia television which broadcast your programme both in 1991 and 1992, and that means that the viewers in Serbia, which means those without satellite dishes, were able to follow the Sky News programme direct and the reports, and therefore were able to become acquainted with the contents of your reports and commentaries, right, both in Croatia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure when it was stopped. I say in the statement up until spring or summer of 1992. Certainly for the whole of 1991 it was shown in Serbia. And correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Milosevic, but I think that's probably one of the reasons why the people in your office advised you to give me interview in July 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the reason was, but I did give a number of interviews. So I assume by the same token that the interview that you're quoting was given that way too. Now, do you agree that Radio-Television Serbia during the period that you're talking about took over not only the information programme of Sky News but also televised part of the CNN programmes, BBC, and other world television channels? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that other channels were broadcast in a similar fashion as Sky News was on the third channel, no. In 1989 when Sky News first went on air, the man then running the third channel, a man called Jaksa Scekic, went to London and made an agreement with the head of Sky News whereby Yugoslav television could have access to Sky News pictures and stories, and Sky News could have access to pictures from Yugoslav television. It was this man, as far as I'm aware, Mr. Scekic, who saw to it that Sky News was then broadcast what I think was 12 hours a day on the third channel. I'm not aware of a similar arrangement with either BBC or CNN. Whether excerpts from BBC or CNN were shown on Serb television is possible, but I don't think they had a similar relationship as the one between Sky News and Yugoslav television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that I don't know about that arrangement between Sky News, but I do know that Sky News was broadcast. Now, what the arrangement was, I don't know, and it's not really important. But doesn't it show quite clearly that there was no intention to create a distorted picture of the events which could be seen on television by viewers in Serbia in view of the fact that you could -- they had an insight into different viewpoints, different reports by foreign television stations about the events in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that might be possible if people were watching the third channel, but I would say that in my personal opinion, the evening news on main the Serb television channels gave a very distorted picture as to what was going on, firstly in the war in Croatia, and then in the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on channel 1 the image was distorted, was it, and on channel 3 they gave an objective view by that same television network? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that in my opinion when I watched and had translated to me what went out on the main news bulletins of Serb television during 1991, 1992, and 1993 was indeed distorted. Sky News was broadcast on the third channel, but the third channel didn't have its own news programme. It showed Sky News in 1991, and I -- we imagined that when that was stopped, it was done for the reason to stop people from getting an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. alternative view, because what was then being shown on Sky News was very different from what was being shown on the main television channel within Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. van Lynden. In any case, it is not in dispute that during 1991 and 1992, Sky News was televised over state television of Serbia. In paragraph 3, you mention an interview that you had with me at the end of July and the beginning of August in 1991, and you place it in that time period. That's when you say it was; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I don't remember the precise date, so it was either the end of July or it was early August 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't remember either having granted you an interview, but I probably did. Possibly I did. So anyway, in that connection, I would like to ask you something. Do you have the footage of the interview between you and me that we could take a look at? It was your interview, so I assume you filmed it and have footage of that interview.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Footage --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or recording.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a personal recording in my personal possession, but it is within the archives of Sky Television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. van Lynden, but don't you think the best testimony about the interview would be the interview itself and then we wouldn't need your words or my words to explain the substance of what I was saying at the time during the interview?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't argue with that, but I -- I mean, that's a question for the Court to bring that tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But you as a journalist, don't you think that it would be within the domain of fair play --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This isn't a matter for the witness. If the tape is available, no doubt it can be made available. But his evidence, you will remember, really related to a conversation outside the main interview.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say in paragraph 3: "I interviewed Slobodan Milosevic. During the interview, he was highly critical of the Albanians in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this does not refer, Mr. May, to what Mr. van Lynden explained a moment ago as to what I said outside the interview, but it refers to the interview itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To explain the position, you ought to know by now there is a distinction between a statement and oral evidence, and it was to the oral evidence to which I was referring. But let us not waste time on these sort of arguments. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. van Lynden, I assume you mean Albanian separatists in Kosovo or Albanian terrorists in Kosovo, not Albanians as such, per se.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember it, it was a comment about the Albanians per se, because the question that I asked you was given the fact that you were demanding that the Serb minority in Croatia were granted certain rights, I then said, "But you are not granting those rights to the Albanian majority in Kosovo," and it was at that point that you said that these two matters could not be compared, that Kosovo was Serb, that it would always remain Serb, and that the position of the Albanians could not be compared to the position of the Serbs in Croatia. You didn't talk about -- as I recall, about Albanian separatists or Albanian terrorists, you just mentioned Albanians as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that can't be possible, because even in the year 2000, Mr. van Lynden, in the Socialist Party of Serbia, whose president I was, in the leadership, there was still Albanians there, even in the year 2000 let alone 1991. So these qualifications could not have referred to the Albanians as a whole but it could have referred exclusively to Albanian separatists. You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked you a question. I remember it, of you talking about the Albanians as a whole, Mr. Milosevic. If you remember it in a different manner, I can't help that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't remember the interview at all, but I do know what I thought at the time, and I know what I think today, and I assume that you know that Yugoslavia was composed of nations, of ethnicities, and members of ethnic minorities as well, and that the Serbs in Croatia had the status of a nation, as they did in Yugoslavia and in Croatia and according to the Croatian constitution, whereas the Albanians had the status of a national minority or a nationality because they had their matrix state in Albania. Was that the case or not, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well have been the case, but we are referring here to a comment you made in an interview with me in 1999 in which you spoke about the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1991, the Albanians were a national minority in Yugoslavia and in Serbia, both pursuant to the constitution of Yugoslavia and the constitution of Serbia. And I assume that you know that very well, because you're a well-informed journalist.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that after the interview I said that the Muslim fundamentalists in Bosnia, and here you quote, "the Vatican papists." Never in my life have I used the term "papist" so I don't know how that term came to be used and I don't think you remember me having used the word "papist" at all.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago that I said that after the break-up of Yugoslavia that Genscher and the Vatican were behind the break-up of Yugoslavia. Is that right? That's what you said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... together. You mentioned a German Fourth Reich and you mentioned Islamic fundamentalists, all in the same sentence, and said that this was a form of conspiracy against the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Genscher in your explanations. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned Genscher and I was quoting you as I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you say that I mentioned Genscher; is that it?
