utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I have here a report from an open television programme, and I asked the Slovenian president, Milan Kucan, a question in that regard, who took part in that particular television programme, and it quotes part of a statement made by the present Croatian president, Stjepan Mesic. Literally I'm reading you the quotation verbatim: "The idea on the break-up of Yugoslavia I wish to convey to those who had the strongest influence on its destiny; Genscher and the Pope. With Genscher I had a meeting three times, and he enabled me to have contacts with the Holy See. The Pope and Genscher agreed with the complete break-up of Yugoslavia." That's what Mesic said at the time in a television broadcast on the 8th of November, 1995, in which Milan Kucan took part as well as some other individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. As you know quite well the witness cannot be asked general questions of that nature unless he has some connection with it. Have you ever come across, Baron, this interview of what Mr. Mesic said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the term "papist" as if I had used it; is that right? As far as I know, that expression is in usage in Great Britain. This is a term I never used.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke English with each other, Mr. Milosevic, as you speak Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. excellent English, and that is what I remember you saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to tell you, Mr. van Lynden, that that is not correct. In fact, I never said anything derogatory about Catholics, and I certainly wouldn't have called them papists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered that. He says -- you apparently have no recollection of the conversation; he says that's his recollection. We will have to consider the significance of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you say, this meant, as you say in your statement, that the war was being waged in predominantly Muslim areas and also in Kosovo, namely, parts of Bosnia and Kosovo; is that right? That is what it says here: "This suggested to me that his ultimate goal was to take the war into predominantly Muslim areas, namely, parts of Bosnia and Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the conclusion that I and my two local producers, one of whom is Serb, came to, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of war in Kosovo in 1991 could have been mentioned at all?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a question of it happening in 1991 but that we expected it to follow the war in Croatia, and it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: This was, you say, in July or beginning of August 1991. What kind of war could have been mentioned in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Because the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I just said, that it would follow. It was an indication to us that war would follow the war that was then being waged in Croatia. And that's what happened. A year later, the war in Bosnia broke out, and later on still, in Kosovo. So we were correct in our analysis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how the war in Bosnia came about?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some idea, yes, and some personal opinions also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep any kind of notes of this conversation? You recorded the interview which you don't have, but I assume we can find it. And then you testify here about a conversation that we had 12 years ago, and from that conversation, you concluded that the war would spread to Bosnia and Kosovo, and you did that in July 1991. Is that what you're claiming, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was an indication to us that this might well happen, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who did you arrange the interview with me with?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was arranged by my local producers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was present during this conversation of ours that you're describing in this way?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I remember, we had two television crews, one from Sky News and one from Belgrade television, because the interview was also shown on Belgrade television. And in fact, large parts of it were published on the front page of papers like Politika the next day. I'm also slightly surprised that you have absolutely no recollection, Mr. Milosevic, because I was informed it was the first interview you gave to a Western journalist. And certainly the two local producers were with us afterwards. I can -- in my remembrance, at the end of the interview you said, "Let's let the technicians deal with the cameras, we will go into a different room." And you also expressed your surprise that while I had been firm in my questioning, I had not been impolite, and to which I think my reply was I was not Oriana Falacci, an Italian journalist well-known for being extremely impolite to political leaders when she interviews them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've read many interviews by Oriana Falacci. I didn't notice that she was impolite. She was a great journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All these people who were present there could confirm, then, what you are claiming regarding our conversation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me -- let us move on to another topic. You spoke about the shelling of Markale, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Sarajevo when that happened. I have already told the Court that I was in Central Bosnia at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But you say that a senior member of Karadzic's staff in February 1994, shortly after the Markale shelling, told me that Seselj this visited Pale. You say that a senior official told you that. Now, who is that senior official? What is his name?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember his name, but I believe that he functioned as a sort of Chief of Staff for Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You speak about an event in the bread line, in paragraph 20, and you say that the Bosnian Serbs claim that the Bosnian forces had opened fire at their own people after the shelling in 1992, a notorious incident when civilians in Sarajevo were shelled waiting to collect bread. Is that right? And you say that that is what the Bosnian Serbs claimed.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what the Bosnian Serbs claimed. I can say one other thing, that I met Dr. Karadzic immediately after the Markale bombing, and he then also claimed that this had been done by the Bosnians rather than by Karadzic's forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in the very next paragraph, I know that that is what the Serbs claimed and that there were many indications that this was a frame-up to blame the Serbs, but already in the next paragraph you say that another person who made such a claim was General Sir Michael Rose, who just before he left Bosnia in an interview with a BBC journalist, John Simpson, in a programme titled Panorama, inferred that some of his senior staff thought that the BiH had shot at their own people. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my remembrance of General Rose's comments to John Simpson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't only that such claims were made on the Serb side, that is, that this had been done by the Muslim side, but General Rose also said that, and he had spent quite a long time in Bosnia-Herzegovina as force commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He'd come to the end of his tenure, one-year tenure as commander of UNPROFOR. He didn't say it outright. He inferred that some of his senior staff thought that it was possible or maybe likely that there had been instances of the Bosnians shooting at their own people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was quite a lot of information about that. Are you familiar with those data?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never -- I have never seen concrete proof from UNPROFOR, despite repeated requests for it, that this indeed occurred. And I have spoken to a number of other people who were in UNPROFOR a lot longer than General Rose who believe that it never happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have occasion to consider the data about this some other time. But tell me, please, you describe Milan Martic's visit to Republika Srpska. Did your own cameramen film the review prepared for Martic or was this something that you borrowed from someone else? I haven't come across that in these CDs.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was indeed filmed by our own cameramen, and I was personally present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. What was Martic in those days?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he styled himself the leader or the president of the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the title he took, yes, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Karadzic, in those days, was President of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what is strange then if Martic comes to visit Karadzic and for Martic to inspect a guard prepared in his honour?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said it was strange. I just simply reported that it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it indicate, this story that Martic came to visit Pale and that he was received with honours and probably had talks after that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with his collocutor Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't made any conclusions from that. I've simply said at that time the Bosnian Serbs got direct support, for instance, from Milan Martic, and we were told that Vojislav Seselj had also come to Pale to voice his support for that position. This was after all after NATO had issued a first ultimatum to the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was in 1994?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in February 1994, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for Seselj's visit, you didn't film that, did you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor did I see him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis, then, are you claiming that Seselj was there at the time?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were told by a senior member of Dr. Karadzic's staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to my information, the only time Seselj went to Pale was to extend support to the citizens of Republika Srpska when NATO bombed their positions in the environs of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then your information differs from mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In January, there was a rally of the Serbian Radical Party which lasted several days, and in February and March, sessions of the Assembly of Serbia attended by Seselj who was a deputy at the time, so that at that date he could not have been at Pale, or he shouldn't have been there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he should or shouldn't is not up for me to decide. And as far as I'm aware, the Serbian parliament doesn't meet during the weekends. As I said, I didn't see him, but we were told by a senior member of Karadzic's staff that he had come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this shelling around Gorazde? Do you recollect that? Do you remember when NATO bombed positions around Gorazde? Was that in 1993?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly have a memory that in April 1994, there was what I believe was an attack by General Mladic's forces on Gorazde during which at least one forward air observer of the British SAS was killed, and there was bombing by NATO planes. I was not in Gorazde at the time. In fact, I was in Belgrade at the time. It was my last days in Serbia because I was then ordered to leave the country after your government decided to call me persona non grata for life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite possible. In paragraph 5, you say that in 1991, you met in Vukovar with a JNA officer, a certain Mladen Maric, captain first class of the Armoured Guards Brigade, and that you spent several days with him and his unit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly when that was?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The precise dates were something between the 10th and the 19th of November, 1991, something like that. It was a ten-day period. We spent one night, a whole night with his unit, slept with them, as I recall around 50 metres from Croat lines, and we visited the city on a daily basis and would find those troops. He was the highest officer, and there was a, as I recall, a Bosnian Muslim lieutenant with him, and a few others. And this was the unit that came under the command of what I think at the time was Major Sljivancanin -- excuse me if I get the pronunciation wrong, it's a difficult name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to the information that I received before you came to testify, and will you please just confirm it is correct; in end October 1991, you had a car accident. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date of the car accident?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: End October. I don't have the precise date. I don't have any earlier information about you. I only have what I received recently. In end October you had a car accident somewhere, and after that, you underwent treatment and spent that time in the Hyatt Hotel. You had a minor concussion or something like that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was at the beginning of October 1992. I had indeed an accident driving with my Land Rover from Hungary to Belgrade, and I think near a place called Novi Beograd I indeed had an accident. But that was 1992, not 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was in 1992. It was not at the time of the siege of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was during the war in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me this, please, since you say that you spent there the last ten days. Does that mean that you were in Vukovar when it fell and that's the time where you were with that captain whom you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have to get permission first from the Defence Ministry in Belgrade. This is something that my local producers did. We get further permission usually in a town called Sid, and then drive on via Tovarnik and a place called Oriolik before turning into Vukovar. Then we were with this unit. We would usually leave Belgrade early in the morning and we would return to Belgrade sometime in the afternoon to then edit our story and send it to London. We didn't always succeed, but as I said, I think something like on the 12th or 13th of November we spent 48 hours in the town, and we were certainly there on a daily basis but not for 24 hours at a time, arriving in the morning, leaving in the afternoon, during the last couple of days of the fighting and after the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you never saw him after that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I do say that I had dinner with him in Belgrade in December 1991, but after that, I never saw him again, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You never saw him again. You say in paragraph 6 of your statement: "I did not see him again, but my producer who was with us in Vukovar told me that on one day in June 1992, he had seen Maric while he was visiting the Lukavica barracks, the headquarters of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. He added that Maric was present during combat operations on the Serb side but was still a member of the JNA, that is, the army of Yugoslavia." That's what it says here. "I am aware that Maric remained with the Serb army, refusing to transfer into the Bosnian Serb army."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether it's a translation matter, but at least the English transcript, as I hear it, does not match the English version of the statement. The reference to JNA in the English version of the statement reads "JNA-VJ." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely how I quoted it, "JNA," that is the army of Yugoslavia. And you can also put it differently, "JNA/VJ," which is how I have it here in the Serbian version, but I quoted every word exactly as it is written, and you can check that on the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thus he says that he had seen Maric visiting the Lukavica barracks and that he was present during combat operations on the Serb side. Now, would you please explain this: On what basis did you claim a moment ago that Maric, whom you say in your statement was described to your cameramen as visiting the Lukavica barracks, was at the head of some JNA unit taking part in some military operations in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you've misunderstood the "whilst visiting." It was my producer who was visiting the Lukavica barracks. He found Maric was stationed there, and he spoke with Maric. I was not present during these conversations. He spoke to Maric, and Maric said that he was on operations there with the JNA. So it was the producer who was visiting, just to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The producer was visiting. And now just on the basis of the presence of a JNA officer who originally comes from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just based on the presence of a JNA officer who is originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina you define that as the presence of the regular Yugoslav army, JNA/VJ in Bosnia, is that so?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was still a guards officer, and he never became an officer in the Bosnian Serb army. He was there as a guards officer of the JNA, and he had his men with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that his men were with him or that he took part in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any operations at all?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only quoting my producer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your producer collected all that information and gave it to you, including information about some sort of operation. What kind of operation did the JNA allegedly take part in in June 1992 in Lukavica, as you say here? What kind of operation was going on then?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already told, I was in Sarajevo at the time, and this producer was based in Pale at the time, and this is what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So this is again something that your producer told you. We will not spend any more time on that. Further on you speak about my statement concerning an embargo and the pressure to accept the peace plan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that this embargo did not cover humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is as I recall it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that the purpose of the embargo was precisely to exert pressure for the peace plan to be accepted?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you said at the time, yes. Whether I believe that is a different matter, but that's the reason you gave for it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. Are you aware of the summit meeting in Athens where Radovan Karadzic signed this peace plan, but it was later rejected at the Assembly meeting of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the Bosnian Serb parliament, as I recall. But I was not present at that meeting. I mean, of -- when the parliament rejected it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind. There is enough information about that session. It was recorded from beginning to end. There's no need to discuss it further. You say that several days after the introduction of the embargo you saw fuel tankers and trucks on this main road, travelling along that main road. I think you mentioned the area surrounding Bijeljina or something like that.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned being in Bijeljina. I saw those trucks crossing over at two different crossings, one at Zvornik and one to the north of Zvornik, and I saw trucks crossing into Bosnian Serb territory. And we noticed that because we were at least told that they were not meant to because there was meant to be an embargo. That's why we noticed it. We saw trucks crossing in 1992 but paid it little heed, but after this introduction of an embargo, we paid it more heed. But it wasn't the purpose. We hadn't gone to the border to see whether the embargo was working. We had gone to go to two places, Janja and Bijeljina, as I recall, to see the voting in the referendum on the decision of the Bosnian Serb Assembly to reject the peace plan that Karadzic, as you said, signed in Athens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's not what I say. He did sign this plan in Athens. So you were there at the time when the embargo had not yet been introduced?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that the embargo had already been introduced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, since you remember that time and maybe we will be able to get more and more precise information about it on some other occasion, do you remember that in relation to that embargo an International Monitoring Mission was deployed along the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska and that that mission was headed by a Swedish General, Bo Pellnas?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember the Swedish General, but I remember that some kind of an outside monitoring observer force was sent, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that this monitoring mission did not draw any conclusions about the embargo being violated? At least I have no information to that effect, while they were on the border all the time after the embargo was introduced, of course, not before. And their presence was made possible only through our goodwill. It was not something that was imposed on us. Because they had asked us, "Are you sincere about this?" We said, "Yes, of course." They said, "Can we monitor this?" We said, "Yes, of course." You are a journalist. You're supposed to know these things?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask the UN. I cannot tell you what the UN thought or did not think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then I shouldn't ask you about this. But if there was a monitoring mission who did their work with all earnestness, don't you suppose that they were able to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This witness testifies that this was all stage-managed. Unfortunately, it wasn't. In paragraph 9, you say that you had to buy fuel for your own cars on the black market in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the case that somebody refused to sell you fuel or was it something that all the citizens of Serbia had to experience because we were under a blockade, under an embargo, suffering great shortages including the shortage of fuel? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But this began in 1991. It was more a question -- there were petrol pumps open with huge queues at them, and if you're working for a 24-hour news channel, you cannot spend hours and hours and hours queueing for fuel to try and get somewhere, because we wouldn't be able to do our work. That's why we decided to set up our own sort of fuel pump -- dump. And this dump was set up before the UN embargo against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But there were shortages. I only wanted to clear up one thing: Nobody targeted or discriminated against you specifically because you were foreigners; but on the contrary, there were queues everywhere and the citizens queued, whereas you didn't have time to. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Citizens indeed queued. Citizens also did the same thing that we did, which was to buy fuel on the black market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only wanted to establish one thing: There was no discrimination against you as a journalist or a foreigner, but you were simply in a situation that was difficult all round in a country.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I was never discriminated upon at any petrol pump in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you are aware under those very hard sanctions that Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina found themselves under. There were no medicines, vaccines, there was no fuel, there were no inputs for the production of medicines either. Everything was blocked. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were medicines. It wasn't that there was no medicine in the whole of Serbia, and it was also not a situation that there was no petrol in the whole of Serbia. There was a huge amount of smuggling going on from neighbouring countries, and that's how we got our petrol and diesel, I imagine, on the black market. Yes, there were shortages, certainly, and for some of the population it was very hard, but if you had your means and you had the money, you could get hold of anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any event, the sanctions were very strict, and it was very difficult to live under them at those times and trade with other countries was, in fact, clandestine, and it was a form of black marketeering, smuggling.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was smuggling, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But of course we did manage to have the minimum quantities of medicines. We did have pharmaceutical factories, so we were able to do something, depending on the success of the smuggling, when it came to the inputs for the pharmaceutical industry and for our factories. I assume you know that too.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, yes, there were medicines available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me this now, please: In paragraph 10, you talk about some sort of regular meetings. So when you say "regular meetings," what do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mean, between Karadzic, Mladic, and myself, meetings that regularly took place, as you say, in Belgrade and on occasions in Pale. Now, what do you mean by these regular meetings?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you will be aware, Mr. Milosevic, I was not attending these meetings, but as I say, we were told -- I was told, my local producers were told by Serb journalists, by other sources, including the head of Belgrade television and a member of the foreign ministry about meetings between you, Dr. Karadzic, and General Mladic took place. And in September 1992, when I met Dr. Karadzic at the Intercontinental Hotel, he told me he was in Belgrade because he was seeing you. I didn't see General Mladic, by the way, at that meeting. I don't know if -- whether he was included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is quite possible that when you saw Karadzic, it was when he came to see me, too, during his stay in Belgrade. But the point of my question was not whether I ever met Karadzic. Of course I did. Or whether I ever met Mladic. Of course I did. But you're talking about some sort of regular meetings. So what do you mean when you say "regular meetings"?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what we were told by the various sources. They wouldn't specify what that meant, whether you were seeing each other once every three days or once every one and a half months, but that there were meetings. That's what we were told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there were meetings, but there couldn't have been regular meetings. And you say sometimes, or you say, "and on occasions in Pale." You know that I was at Pale only once, to attend an Assembly of Republika Srpska when the Vance Owen plan was on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that you visited Pale then. Again, I am quoting others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say "in Pale," that cannot be correct at all, can it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I'm quoting others, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that you're quoting others, but it would appear that those sources were not the most reliable. And you also say that in Pale, you had several meetings with Karadzic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume you had an interview with him.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time, no. These were just meetings to talk to each other. Dr. Karadzic very much wanted to do interviews directly with Sky News, either, if we had a satellite dish, by standing in front of the camera; or if we did not have a satellite dish, then via the telephone. We had meetings in which we simply had conversations about what was happening in Bosnia. I did, on occasion, go there also to ask him a few questions, but they weren't this kind of formal 40-minute, sit-down interviews. Those would be sessions that would last five or ten minutes when I just had a couple of questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have five minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. If I have just five more minutes, then I'm going to shorten all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your presentation yesterday, you mentioned snipers. As far as I know, there were snipers on both sides.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall presenting anything yesterday, but, yes, there were snipers on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that it was read out from the summary, actually. The summary of your statement was read out. I'm not saying that you said this yesterday; you were quoted as having said that. From the previous statement, that's the note that I made of it. But anyway, the snipers existed on both sides. Isn't that right, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the Serb side, too, you saw shelters put up against snipers, barriers to protect the people from Muslim snipers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's in my statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said yesterday or were quoted as saying yesterday, I can't remember which it was, but anyway, it was said that the snipers chose their own targets. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that snipers in the positions that I was taken to in Grbavica told me that they chose their own targets, but what we also saw was that there were radios and that there were what we would call spotters or observers who were at different, I imagine higher locations, informing the snipers. I have to add that I had never went with a unit on the other side, and therefore, I cannot describe how their snipers behaved, but they certainly had them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you that because a witness here claimed that that sniper fire from Serb positions was coordinated from the top echelons; whereas, what you said would make it appear different. You mentioned having seen mortars at the -- by the Kosevo hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw one mortar by the Kosevo hospital in July 1992, yes, but without any troops there, just the mortar. As I recall, an 82 or 81-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You're a war reporter. You can differentiate between weapons. You saw a mortars by the Kosevo hospital, and it belonged to the Muslims, didn't it? It was a Muslim mortar.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mortar which I imagine belonged to the Bosnian army, which was never a Muslim army in my opinion, because I always encountered Serbs and Croats in that army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Anyway, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, did they open fire? Do you know that they used the hospital as a shelter to or vantage point to open fire at the army of Republika Srpska from?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in July 1992 when there wasn't yet a Republika Srpska, first point. Secondly, no, I never saw that mortar actually fire. And I never saw fire emanating from the hospital terrain in Sarajevo. Certainly never at the state hospital where I spent many nights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just two more questions, please, if I may. I hope I'm going to have time for that, Mr. May. You spoke about the conflict at the Dvor na Uni. You spoke about that towards the end of today's presentation, I believe.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked about Dvor na Uni, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who fell victim during that clash at Dvor na Uni?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you're referring to either the fighting in the village of Struga or the incident in Dvor na Uni between Captain Dragan and the local population. If you're referring to what happened in Struga, as far as I can remember, four inhabitants of Struga, all Croat, were killed, and two Serb militiamen. If you're referring to the incident in Dvor na Uni itself, Captain Dragan told me that the ten Serbs that he had arrested had killed four Croat women who came from Struga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, and that's why I'm asking you. When did that take place, actually?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: July 1991, you say. And then this was the final question you were asked and your final response during the examination-in-chief: You claim that Captain Dragan told you that I was in charge of all those operations. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He never said that you were operationally in charge. What he told me was that you were the ultimate leader of the Serbs. And when I have asked that question to -- to Dr. Karadzic or General Mladic, they wouldn't have argued with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Okay. That I was the Serb occupying the highest position. That is not at issue, because I was president of the Republic of Serbia. But that's quite another matter, quite different from what I understood you to say in response to a question asked by the other side as to who was in charge of these operations and that Dragan told you that it was Milosevic who was in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has answered. He said what -- he told you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what Captain Dragan said. Yes. Now -- now, what is -- Mr. Milosevic, what is the point you want to make? You've got your answer. He's told you what Dragan said about you. Now, what is your final point, and it is your final point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my question was precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The year 1991, the month of July, is it true Mr. van Lynden that at that time there was the JNA presence as a legal army there, as a legitimate army of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and we're talking about July 1991, and you yourself said that they had come after the conflicts to set up a buffer zone there.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about 1991. Yes, the JNA was there as the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And yes, in the village of Struga they had come to set up a buffer after the fighting had stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Have -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have exhausted your time. We have got well beyond the time that you should have been allow. Have the amici any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I have about ten or 15 minutes of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Make a start then, please. Questioned by Mr. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a topic that I would like to broach to start off with, and I have questions in that regard, and that's the one I would need most time for. But perhaps I could start with somebody else first up to the break and then carry on. Baron, when you spoke about the hospital and what you did from the roof of the hospital, in paragraph 12 you said that with a cameraman and sound man, you would record from the top building of the hospital and from a sheltered place you would watch the fire across the city coming from both sides of the hospital. So at that time, there were no operations vis-a-vis you who were conducting your -- doing your job there. And I'm referring to paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should just add, Your Honours, I was never on the roof. That would not have been a very sensible place to be. I was on the top floor of the hospital. I don't quite understand what you mean by "operations vis-a-vis you." What do you mean by "operations"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point in time, was there firing at the hospital from any side? That's what I wanted to ask you; was the hospital fired at from any side while you were up there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite regularly the hospital was fired at while we were in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next sentence, you say the cameraman and sound man would swap sides according to the pattern of fire in order to record it. Does that mean with respect to the fire opened at the hospital, targeting the hospital?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not, because you cannot -- it's very, very difficult to film anyway. No. This is talking about filming shelling of either the eastern or western halves of Sarajevo. And if we felt that it was heavier in the east, then the cameraman would go to the side of the building that faced towards that direction. That's what it's a reference to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at any case, in that particular point -- at that particular point in time it wasn't the hospital that was targeted by this fire.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital would also be hit, but it wasn't -- filming shelling, a television filming of shelling is incredibly difficult, because artillery shelling you don't see. It is much easier when it is multiple rocket launcher fire because you can see the rockets, but you can't see the artillery shell. And one shell lands there, and if the other shell lands there, you may still be filming. You can only start filming when the first shell has landed. It's a complicated thing. Therefore, to film a single shot or a couple of rounds coming into the hospital building would be completely impossible. Apart from that, I have to say that at any time that I was in the building, the only time that it was hit by a heavier shell was when it was hit by what I think - what we think - was a tank shell. But at that time I was in the basement, waiting to take the lift up to the higher floors. So the only fire that I witnessed when on the upper floors was of lower-calibre fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me this, please: While you were in the building, new casualties kept coming in, as you say in paragraph 13. Now, during those points in time while you were there and the hospital was hit, did anybody fall casualty while you were there?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall two people were wounded inside the hospital at a lower floor when I was on the upper floor, but we only heard about that later. I don't recall either of them being seriously hurt, but those were people working on the lower floors. All the upper floors of the hospital had been evacuated, and the only people residing on the top floor was the Sky News crew. But yes, there were casualties there, and I was informed that prior to my arrival others had been hit inside the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment, Mr. Tapuskovic? Very well. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic. We understand that you've been taken unwell. If that's right, you can leave while we conclude this witness. Do you want to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. May, you know full well that for many months now I have no conditions to rest, and it's just a question of increased blood pressure due to fatigue. I don't believe I'm ill. It's simply this fatigue that contributes to higher blood pressure, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will finish the witness. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I was asking you those things a moment ago because there are two other statements that you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal in 2001 and 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Excuse me. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked the Prosecution if they would be kind enough to give you copies in front of you so that I might ask for a few explanations from you for the benefit of Their Honours. In this first statement from 2001, it is the chapter headed "Shelling of Hospitals." And you said here, in the middle of that chapter, third paragraph from the end: "I am aware of the allegation that the hospital was shelled only because the Bosnians used it as a sniping position, though I cannot categorically say that that was not the case." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that in the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fifth paragraph in this chapter.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by what I told the investigator at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the chapter "Shelling of Civilian Emergency Services," and when the building where the firemen were extinguishing the fire is mentioned, in the third paragraph, somewhere in the middle you say: "I saw that the firemen were managing to put the fire out in a part of the building. However, the Serb gunners succeeded in setting another part alight. Thought we cannot exclude the possibility that ABiH snipers were using this building, this attack cannot be considered a justifiable military action."

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, we asked people living -- living in the apartment whether this building had been used for any military purposes whatsoever that could have given rise to this building coming under attack. We were told by those people that it had not been. And I think I should point out to the Court that civilians living Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in Sarajevo by that stage realised full well that if a building was used that it could come under attack and what the consequences for their property would be. So I cannot exclude it. I asked the questions. We also went to UNPROFOR and asked them, after this incident, whether they had seen or whether either any of their forces or observers had noted any fire coming from this building being directed toward Serb lines, and they said they had not. The third thing that made me feel that this was a very odd incident indeed was that only incendiary bullets were used. Now, in any kind of normal military engagement, certainly one where both sides were fighting at each other, you would have all sorts of calibre of weapons being used. On this occasion, the only fire that I saw hitting this apartment block was of incendiary bullets. Therefore, I felt it was a direct attack on a civilian target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you hear from UNPROFOR representatives, the officers in the first place, that in some cases UNPROFOR bases were used in such a way that close to those bases certain armed formations would be positioned, armed formations of the BiH army who would open fire on Serb positions from there? Had you heard of any provocations from the city of Sarajevo towards those that were besieging Sarajevo? Did you hear any such reports?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember any UNPROFOR officer or spokesman telling me that during my time in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Baron, could you please look at your statement of 2002, the chapter dealing with Vukovar. You have already referred to it in the examination-in-chief. Now, could you please look at the second paragraph of that chapter, somewhere in the middle. Speaking about Vukovar you said the following: "Sometimes the JNA would take us in armoured vehicles. Sometimes we would use our own vehicles, but more frequently the latter. Only towards the fall of Vukovar did we get good access is to Vukovar through the Guards Unit of the JNA." Is that right? Does that mean that the Yugoslav People's Army was ready to give you full access to the events taking place just prior to the fall of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on which part of the Yugoslav army you contacted. We had days that we actually met a general of the Yugoslav army outside of Vukovar who gave us permission to go in and that when we arrived in a small village called Oriolik, there would be some Commissar from the Yugoslav army who would not allow us to go any further and sent us back. We nearly always had to get permission first from the Ministry of Defence in Belgrade, then in Sid, and then it just depended who you ran into. When I said that we got better access towards the end, it was because we were facilitated by those officers in the Guards Unit once we made it into Vukovar. But getting into Vukovar, every day you didn't know, even if you had permission, whether you would get in or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in any event, just before the fall of Vukovar, you could -- you had full insight into the developments in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say I had full insight. I never saw the operational maps on the Yugoslav army side. I of course didn't have any contact with the Croatian side whatsoever. We tried to have as full an insight by going into the town and as I also explained already to the Court, on one night we spent a night sleeping with the guard soldiers some 50 metres from Croat lines which, I should add, was pretty dangerous. So we tried to get as full an insight as possible, but a complete insight, no, of course not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, but two paragraphs lower down, you refer to a captain of the Guards Unit who complained to you that the JNA was having two many casualties in that area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was Mladen Maric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is what you say in the next paragraph at the end of it also true, that when you entered the town there were mines everywhere, even in the centre of town? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we filmed them being cleared by soldiers of the JNA after the town had -- yes. So we encountered minefields in the centre of town, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also is the following correct that you stated at the end of the next paragraph: "Together with the army, we went on a trip outside Vukovar where the Croats surrendered. This group of Croatians were not in uniform. As they came out, each man laid down his arms, whatever he had. They were then frisked and led to buses organised by the JNA. There was no jeering or shouting. Some of the Croats were crying, some were trying to keep their heads held high." Do you remember that scene?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that story is in the hands of the Tribunal. This wasn't just soldiers. I should say there was civilians as well. There were women, all the people coming out of Vukovar. There were several thousand people walking out of Vukovar, but that scene is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were civilians from whom weapons were seized, among others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the -- they were all in civilian clothing. Some of them had weaponry, some of them did not. There were also old women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Then we come to the next paragraph where you say in the last sentence: "We saw a huge mass of people leaving. They were all civilians. The JNA were guarding them, protecting them from getting harassed by the Serb paramilitary units. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see what it says towards the end of your statement: "For a while after that, buses arrived to evacuate the remaining Croats. We accompanied the convoy as far as Sremska Mitrovica. I remember that the JNA accused the Croatian forces outside Vukovar of shooting at this convoy. The convoy spent the night in Sremska Mitrovica and the next day via Bosnia it went off to Croatia." Is that also true?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more point in connection with Karadzic. Today during your examination-in-chief, you said, and this is your first statement, the chapter dealing with Karadzic where you explain the reference that you made to the Berlin Wall. You said that this was a conversation that you had with him in September 1992. Was that the conversation when he showed you the maps?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were various conversations in which he showed me the maps. This was held in his office, this meeting, when he spoke about the Berlin Wall. We had generally meetings within his office, but we also had one meeting at the headquarters of the television in Pale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall that when there was a discussion as to the ownership of the Serbs, was it stated that according to the cadastre, according to official documents which are the only things that can prove right of ownership -- this was not a question of the nation but the cadastre, according to which 65 per cent of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in the ownership of Serbs. Was that mentioned?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite possibly, but I don't recall that he used the word "cadastre," no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question: As you said that there was a reference to the Berlin Wall, which is, of course, quite inappropriate civilisation-wise, but you spoke about another meeting in September 1992 and the maps that were shown on that occasion. But on that occasion there was no mention of the Berlin Wall. I don't know whether that was the same meeting, I'd like you to explain that, but the last sentence, if you look at the last paragraph of the second statement, "Command Control..." it says that: "He said that he wanted Yugoslavia because it was a country for the life of all Serbs. He was not talking about any separation or division. He was saying that he favoured or that he wanted representatives of other peoples to move away but that he wanted Yugoslavia as it was a country enabling life for everyone. And on another occasion, he spoke about the partition of Sarajevo." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is what you said here correct? And that would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're jumping from one statement to another very, very quickly, so excuse me if I just read it now. Yes, with Yugoslavia being defined as a Greater Serbia, a state that did not have any Croats, Muslims, or anything else in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Baron, that doesn't -- that's not stated in your statement, because if he had said that, surely you would have said so. What you're saying now cannot be found in your statement. How can you explain that, that you never mentioned the word "Greater Serbia," on that occasion? Because that would be very important for the investigators and for drawing any or making any determinations about anything.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said was that the enclaves were unacceptable and that they had to become part of Serb territory without the inhabitants of those enclaves staying. So in that sense, I mean a Greater Serbia. I mean, those are my words. It means all the Serb territories should be together. That, to him, meant Yugoslavia in the sense that you see it there; that Yugoslavia was a state for all the Serbs to live in, not the Yugoslavia of Slovenes, Croats, Muslims, Albanians, and Serbs -- Montenegrins and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, paragraph 19, if I may refer to it, where you speak about uniforms.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which statement? Which statement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your last statement, Witness, in 2003, paragraph 40. You said here -- you corrected yourself, and you said: "In my first statement, I referred to the uniforms worn by these soldiers as being the same kind of uniform as the Yugoslav army wore the previous year. They were JNA uniforms as worn by the JNA that I saw during the fighting in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me which paragraph you're reading from, as this has only just been handed to me. Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were referring to the uniforms you saw worn by the JNA in Vukovar where you had been a year before, but you said at the end that the Red Star had been replaced with a Serbian tricoloured cap badge. So from the moment you followed events in Bosnia, there were no longer JNA uniforms but these other uniforms were worn. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The uniform was the same, the cap badge was different. All the ranks were the same, everything was the same apart from the cap badge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the cap itself, was it the same? Was it completely different, a completely different cap specific only to the army of Republika Srpska? For example, General Mladic, what kind of cap did he wear?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going back to 1992, he wore JNA uniform. He changed it, or they changed it later on, but that was only later on. In 1992 they were still wearing JNA uniforms. In you check, you'll find that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Sky News was no longer broadcast in Serbia following a decision to close it down. When was that?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Sky News wasn't closed down. It was decided by the Serb authorities no longer to broadcast Sky News 12 hours a day on the third channel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some stage in 1992. I'm not aware of any precise date, but as far as I can remember, it was at the beginning or in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that your evidence on the subject of the snipers operating from Grbavica was inconsistent with the notion that their operations were coordinated from the top levels of the Bosnian Serb army. Were these soldiers wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you gain access to them?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through company or battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you make contact with those company or battalion commanders?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: After meeting General Mladic and after he had given his accord that I could visit military units under his command on the various front lines around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you accompanied by anyone when you spoke to the company or battalion commanders?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, Dr. Karadzic had arranged that two Serb military policemen accompanied us as all times if we left Pale, and they did so. And at certain moments, although I don't think in 1992 but certainly in 1994, when I visited similar units in Grbavica, there was someone from the Bosnian Serb government, usually some press officer of one sort or another who would accompany us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed did those two military policemen arrange the contact between you and the company or battalion commanders?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect that it was usually arranged beforehand from the headquarters in Pale, but they knew who to go to and who to contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were also taken to one of your statements where you said in effect that you were aware of a suggestion that fire by Bosnian Serb forces against the state hospital was in response to sniping from the hospital. Where did that suggestion come from? Where did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see in the state hospital forces of the Bosnian army in operation?

utterances.speaker: AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw them being operated on. No, we never saw any armed soldiers from the Bosnian army in the hospital. And I should add one point to Your Honours here. As the correspondent, one is in charge of a team and, therefore, also in effect responsible for the people in that team. Of course in a war zone, you are always -- there is a certain threat that something may happen to one member of your team or another, but I was quite careful with the cameraman with whom I'd already worked for many years to check quite carefully through the top floors of that building to see if we found any empty cartridges, for instance, any kind of sign that the building had been used for military purposes, and we never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That completes re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Baron van Lynden, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've made some inquiries in relation to the contents of the CD that the accused has indicated was blank. I do apologise for that. It transpires, as I understand it, that Mr. Kay also received a blank CD. His was replaced. We were unaware that one was provided to the accused. However, I can indicate that the contents were identical to annex A being a CD annexed to the 92 bis (A) statement of the accused, so one way or another he has received the contents. Your Honour, also for the record, might I say that I have been assisted by Prashanthi Mahindaratne in the presentation of the evidence for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have to look at that. You might also, Mr. Ierace, while you're at it, see if you can lay hands on the interview which the witness conducted with Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the OTP does not possess a copy of that. We will need to seek it from the Sky News, Sky Television organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Maybe you could get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, given the accused's condition, we will consider what to do next. Are there any matters, administrative matters that anybody wants to raise before any witness is called or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not really, only to say that we have circulated by way of a memorandum, which I hope is acceptable, a list of rather abbreviated format, a list of the witnesses to be called and the witnesses who need not be prepared, and I only say that again so that the accused can understand what that piece of paper is. In particular, the list that tells him the witnesses need not be prepared identifies witnesses we do not now expect to have time to call and so he can stand down preparation for them. In light of his earlier observation about the strains on him of the work that he's having to do, I hope he will find this a helpful guide to his work. We will provide, incidentally, the same list in a fuller form but it's subject to some editorial work at the moment and I want it to come to you in a final form as soon as can be. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, you're feeling tired; is that right? What's your condition?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have told you, Mr. May. I have been tired for months now, and it's no news to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may have been that it's the task which you've taken in hand which is proving so much for you. Have you considered that? Do you need assistance in it? This is a very considerable trial. If you had assistance, you wouldn't be feeling the strain so much, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, there is no assistance that can help me listen to thousands of videotapes and half a million pages while being present here for examination-in-chief and cross-examination. I hope that is clear to you. As far as Mr. Nice's remark is concerned about some sort of memo, I don't know what memo he's talking about because I never received any. And as regards the blank CD being identical to the CD containing annex A, I wish to note that I received annex A when this witness started to testify, together with the background material that is usually given to me just before the testimony, and I was able to see it only last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What I had in mind was that you should have legal representation, as you've been told from the very beginning, but that is a matter for you, and we'll have to decide what course is appropriate. Anyway, we'll not continue today in the circumstances. The registrar has a point about an exhibit number. Let's deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The exhibit you were -- Your Honour, the CD-ROM used by Mr. Milosevic will be Defence Exhibit 192 and Prosecution number is V000-0870 to 0871.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of September, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
